tactics.claim: When the product's differentiator is an identity attribute rather than a visible result, build the visual beats as exaggerated everyday feats that embody that attribute — grilling through a thunderstorm, forcing open a stuck pickle jar with an 'arghhh' face — keep the product out of those frames entirely, and reveal the full product lineup only in the final shot.
tactics.mechanism: An identity claim like 'dad strength' cannot be demonstrated on the product itself, so the frames dramatise the trait through unrelated ordinary situations the buyer recognises. Because the product is absent, the viewer reads the scenes as entertainment rather than advertising and is still watching when the reveal lands.
tactics.evidence: Assertion only; carried entirely by the worked Dr. Squatch 'Dad Strength' example sequence.

rscFit.reasoning: Natural deodorant and soap are the canonical case where the differentiator is non-demonstrable — the existing product-image-stack rule is to relegate non-demonstrable attributes to text, and this supplies a visual route for them instead, a real addition rather than a restatement. It is also the concrete production method for the already-recorded 'give the product a role the buyer gets to display' principle, and one person with an image model can shoot it today.

targetSkill.name: marketing-product-image-stack
targetSkill.description: Add dramatising a non-demonstrable identity attribute as exaggerated everyday feats with the product absent until the final reveal.

tactics.claim: Learn AI ad creation so you can sell it as a service — put businesses on a $500–$1,000/month retainer producing weekly or monthly image and video ads for them.
tactics.mechanism: Most businesses lack the time, skill or money to do it themselves, so a creator who can is selling a recurring need rather than a one-off deliverable.
tactics.evidence: Assertion only; creator says 'we've seen it in our own business and we've seen it in a ton of our client businesses'.

rscFit.reasoning: B2B service pricing with no honest translation to an ecommerce catalogue at any size.

tactics.rejectReason: This is agency offer-building and retainer pricing — a different business, not a bigger version of RSC. Not a scale or headcount problem, so it cannot be parked either.

tactics.claim: Make the ad visually shocking, scary or funny — something people are not used to seeing, like riding an eagle or appearing as a TV character — and now that AI makes production cheap, take bigger visual swings with the same script (deliver it while skydiving or hunting dinosaurs rather than at a desk).
tactics.mechanism: Attention is the gate: no amount of product or messaging quality matters if the viewer never stops, and once the script formula is solved the visual presentation is the remaining differentiator — AI removes the cost constraint that used to cap visual ambition.
tactics.evidence: Creator shows two of his own surreal ads (eagle, The Boys character) and says the process produced ads working well; the bigger-swings claim is assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: Relevant in substance but already held, and partly motivational framing.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of recorded claims: marketing-paid-creative-testing already holds placing every static concept at one end of the clarity spectrum (uber-clear or deliberately surreal purely to stop the scroll) and giving the image exactly one job, and the actionable core of the bigger-swings version — hold the script and audio fixed, change only the visuals with AI — is also already recorded. Re-adding would degrade skill triggering.

tactics.claim: Every ad must call out a specific problem the product solves or a burning desire it fulfils, because that is the only reason anyone ever buys anything.
tactics.mechanism: Buyers act from a live problem or desire, so an ad that names theirs gets read as relevant and one that does not gets scrolled past.
tactics.evidence: Pest-control and course-buyer examples; assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: True but wholly covered by existing skills.

tactics.rejectReason: Already covered multiple times: marketing-awareness-level-messaging ranks candidate desires and checks the winner is a pain felt today, and marketing-problem-solution-inventory enumerates every problem in the buyer's sequence and inverts each into what the asset must say.

tactics.claim: Describe your simple ad idea to ChatGPT — or hand it a reusable fill-in prompt template for scenes and products — and have it write the long, detailed generation prompt you paste into the image model.
tactics.mechanism: Detailed prompts outperform rough ones, and an LLM will expand a one-line idea into the specific scene, lighting, props and emphasis language the image model responds to, while the template carries the technical constraints you always want so none is forgotten.
tactics.evidence: Demonstrated several times (course box ad, roofing before/after, scene and product templates with back-and-forth in Claude); 'I did not write that by hand myself'.

rscFit.reasoning: Right practice, already recorded in a sharper form.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate: marketing-ai-product-imagery already holds 'have the LLM turn the already-approved story into several numbered image-generation concepts, then paste each generation prompt into the image tool' plus the structured SCENE/SUBJECT/EMOTIONAL READ concept pass, and already resolves the tension with its own short-plain-prompt claim. The only genuinely new content (fixed field order, three-quarter angle) is adopted as its own tactics.

tactics.claim: Build the ad as a side-by-side before/after split screen — the destroyed state on the left, the fixed state on the right — so the problem and the solution are both visible in one frame.
tactics.mechanism: A split frame shows the problem and the result simultaneously, which communicates the transformation without the viewer reading any copy.
tactics.evidence: Demonstrated for a hypothetical roofing client ('Storm damage. We can help.'); assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: Already held in a better-calibrated form.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of marketing-product-image-stack: 'Show the transformation rather than describing the after-state — and where an honest before/after does not exist, build the frame as a routine contrast instead', plus the required transformation formats and the prescribed gallery slot for a before/after. The existing version is better calibrated for RSC, where an honest deodorant before/after usually does not exist.

tactics.claim: Set the batch quantity to two or four so every prompt returns several versions, then pick the best one.
tactics.mechanism: Generation is stochastic, so multiple outputs per prompt give you a choice at no extra workflow cost and avoid re-prompting to escape a bad roll.
tactics.evidence: Demonstrated throughout (two generations per static, four versions of the character).

rscFit.reasoning: A settings-panel restatement of a rule already recorded.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of marketing-ai-product-imagery, which already holds that you should expect to discard more generations than you keep and generate several options before choosing.

tactics.claim: AI lets you make a $300,000-quality, professional-looking ad in one day for under $100 — or under $30 — in credits, because it removes the need for actors, expensive cameras, writers and a visual effects team, so you can test more ideas and get feedback faster.
tactics.mechanism: Cheaper, faster asset production means more creative shots on goal per month; no mechanism stated beyond the cost comparison.
tactics.evidence: Creator's own stated cost and timeline for the demo ads; assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: Framing for why the course matters rather than an executable tactic.

tactics.rejectReason: No instruction, threshold or testable step — the actionable content sits in the specific workflow tactics extracted separately, and 'produce creative yourself with AI instead of hiring' is already recorded in marketing-ai-product-imagery.

tactics.claim: Write the script by asking ChatGPT to follow a named competitor's storytelling formula — strong hook, humour and education around the product, then a call to action — after having it generate candidate product angles to pick from.
tactics.mechanism: The model drafts against a structure that is already proven in the category instead of inventing one, so the output inherits the pattern rather than generic ad language.
tactics.evidence: Demonstrated: ChatGPT asked for funny Dr. Squatch product ideas, then asked to write a 30-second script following the Dr. Squatch formula.

rscFit.reasoning: Identical instruction to two recorded claims with a different example substituted.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate: marketing-competitor-messaging-teardown already holds briefing an LLM off a surviving ad to produce your own version of its structure, and marketing-copy-body-structure holds 'Don't brief the model cold — look up the canonical published structure for the format you are writing and have it draft against that structure'.

tactics.claim: Treat the storyboard as the foundation of the whole piece because the process is image-to-video — every image you generate is literally the start frame of a clip, and starting from a high-resolution still almost guarantees a good-looking clip.
tactics.mechanism: Clip quality is inherited from the input frame, so resolution and composition of the start image dominate the output and the frames are where the quality decisions get made.
tactics.evidence: Asserted as the reason storyboarding matters, plus repeated-use assertion: 'if you start with a high resolution image, you're almost guaranteed to get a great looking video out of it'.

rscFit.reasoning: Correct and relevant but already recorded verbatim in substance.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of marketing-ai-broll-generation: 'the image model makes the frames and the video model only animates them... because clip quality is decided almost entirely by the start frame you feed it'. Re-recording would degrade skill triggering.

tactics.claim: Hold character consistency across every scene by feeding the same generated character image into each scene prompt as the base.
tactics.mechanism: Consistent inputs produce consistent outputs, so the character reference carried into each generation keeps the person identical scene to scene.
tactics.evidence: Demonstrated throughout the build.

rscFit.reasoning: Already held.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of marketing-ai-broll-generation: 'carry the same reference image into every thread rather than relying on the model's memory' and 'do the production in a fixed order — characters first, environments second, product last'.

tactics.claim: Relabel the product inside a generated image — swap the real product in and then prompt 'change the name of the soap from Wood Barrel Bourbon to Dad Strength' — to create the SKU the ad concept needs.
tactics.mechanism: The image model will rewrite packaging text on request, so the creative concept is not limited to products that exist and the fix is a cheap edit rather than a Photoshop job.
tactics.evidence: Demonstrated on the generated soap bar and supplied as a working prompt in the course doc.

rscFit.reasoning: Duplicates a recorded edit move and conflicts with a recorded compliance guardrail.

tactics.rejectReason: marketing-ai-product-imagery already holds the identical text-replacement edit plus a proofreading pass, and marketing-product-image-stack holds that a generated render must match the real product exactly or the listing gets taken down. Inventing packaging the business does not sell invites a compliance takedown and a buyer who receives something other than what they saw.

tactics.claim: Do the assembly in a free desktop editor such as DaVinci Resolve.
tactics.mechanism: A free, widely-taught editor is enough for this work, so tool cost is not a barrier.
tactics.evidence: Assertion plus use throughout the demonstration; creator notes 'you don't have to use DaVinci Resolve' and points to his own paid course for mastering it.

rscFit.reasoning: Tool-name restatement of an existing claim.

tactics.rejectReason: Already covered: marketing-short-form-video-production holds the claim to edit in a basic editor (Reels native or CapCut) rather than auto-editing templates or one-shot AI editors. Swapping in another tool name restates it and would blur triggering.

tactics.claim: Every profitable ad runs the same five elements in order: hook, problem, solution, offer, call to action.
tactics.mechanism: Each element earns the right to the next — attention, then demonstrated understanding, then the solution in the customer's own language, then stacked value, then an explicit next step.
tactics.evidence: Asserted as 'the formula', then demonstrated on his own AI Creator Course ad read start to finish.

rscFit.reasoning: Sound and durable, but a thinner version of a recorded skeleton.

tactics.rejectReason: marketing-copy-body-structure already holds the six-step skeleton (problem/want, mechanism, why your mechanism is better, result, bridge the skepticism, call to action) — the same sequence with the proof and objection beats spelled out more fully. Re-adding a thinner version would degrade triggering.

tactics.claim: Test the same ad body with several different hooks, because changing one or two opening lines can turn an underperforming ad into the highest performer in the account.
tactics.mechanism: The hook decides whether the rest of the ad is seen at all, so it carries disproportionate variance; holding the body constant isolates it.
tactics.evidence: Reports it as a repeated pattern in his own account ('it doesn't just do a little bit better, it'll become the highest performing ad in our account').

rscFit.reasoning: Correct and relevant but already recorded twice.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate — hook-swap testing against a fixed body is already held in the existing creative-testing and copy skills.

tactics.claim: In the problem section, prove you understand the viewer's situation to the point that you could write a day in their diary — neither vague and surface-level nor explained like a PhD scientist — because people only trust solutions from people who understand their problem.
tactics.mechanism: Demonstrated understanding is what buys the right to pitch; vagueness reads as generic and over-technical explanation reads as not-for-me.
tactics.evidence: Assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle, already held.

tactics.rejectReason: Already recorded — describing the buyer's problem in extreme detail to earn the right to pitch is held in the credibility and awareness-level skills. The 'diary' phrasing is a nice articulation, not a new mechanism.

tactics.claim: Frame a desire as a problem the viewer is currently in, because pain motivates action more than the desire to gain something.
tactics.mechanism: If someone wants something and does not have it, that gap is itself a problem; stating it as present pain creates motive to act now rather than aspiration to act someday.
tactics.evidence: Assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable and true, already recorded.

tactics.rejectReason: Already held as negative framing and as the dual-direction angle inventory in the existing copy skills.

tactics.claim: Only mention what the customer already perceives as valuable — if you know something is a major benefit but the customer does not see it as valuable, leave it out of the ad entirely.
tactics.mechanism: Copy space spent on benefits the buyer does not register is wasted and signals that you are talking about yourself rather than them.
tactics.evidence: Assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: Right, and already covered from both directions.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate — the existing angle and messaging skills already rank claims by buyer-perceived value and instruct cutting the ones the buyer does not register.

tactics.claim: Add a guarantee as an enhancer — at minimum a refund policy, and at the advanced end a results- or speed-based guarantee such as a finished website in under a week.
tactics.mechanism: A guarantee lowers the stress of buying, which pushes a marginal buyer over the edge.
tactics.evidence: Assertion with one hypothetical example.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable and relevant but already held in more operational form.

tactics.rejectReason: Already recorded, including how to structure a guarantee by ticket size — this version adds no new mechanism.

tactics.claim: Fill in a thorough offer worksheet, then prompt ChatGPT with 'act as a professional ad copywriter... write a high-converting Facebook ad in my personal writing style using the Hook, Problem, Solution, Offer, Call to Action framework, emotionally engaging, under 150 words' and paste the completed worksheet beneath it.
tactics.mechanism: The worksheet is the compass — without that context the model guesses — and naming the framework in the prompt forces the output into the structure that converts.
tactics.evidence: The exact prompt and a pre-filled example worksheet are provided as course resources; he reads out a resulting ad.

rscFit.reasoning: Right practice, already recorded twice.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of the recorded positioning interview and persistent project brief claims; the only new element is the specific prompt wording.

tactics.claim: Create a dedicated ChatGPT Project and paste the completed worksheet into its custom instructions, so that any hook or outline you drop in afterwards is automatically written up as a full ad against that brief.
tactics.mechanism: Project-level instructions persist, so the brief never has to be re-pasted and every future ad inherits the same positioning.
tactics.evidence: Demonstrated with the exact instruction text.

rscFit.reasoning: Already held verbatim.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate — the persistent project brief in LLM custom instructions is already a recorded claim.

tactics.claim: Treat length as a prompt variable — change 'under 150 words' to 'under 500 words' in the same prompt to get a much more detailed version of the same ad.
tactics.mechanism: The brief and framework stay fixed, so the word-count constraint alone dials the asset between short-form and long-form placements.
tactics.evidence: Assertion ('it's a very modular process').

rscFit.reasoning: A prompt detail rather than a tactic, and it conflicts with a sharper recorded principle.

tactics.rejectReason: Conflicts with the recorded principle that length is angle count — you lengthen or shorten by adding or cutting angles, not by asking the model for more words.

tactics.claim: Lay a foundation for the model rather than letting it originate: write the hook yourself (or an outline with the specific points, such as a new customer result, that you want included), paste it in, and have the LLM build out the rest of the ad from the standing brief — recycling the back half of a proven ad and changing only the hook.
tactics.mechanism: The hook carries most of the variance and is the part a human does better; the body is formulaic once the brief exists, so human effort concentrates where it pays and the model handles assembly.
tactics.evidence: Says it is the strategy he uses most often, with the '$6 AI ad that generated $50,000' hook as a worked example.

rscFit.reasoning: The right division of labour for a solo operator — which is why it is already recorded.

tactics.rejectReason: Both halves — write the hook yourself and have the LLM assemble the body from a standing brief, and swap only the hook on a proven body — are already recorded claims.

tactics.claim: Remix winners: paste the script of an ad that is performing or has performed well and prompt 'analyze this script and write a new and unique ad that builds off the same concept', then ask for three to four more hook variations made as shocking or interesting as possible.
tactics.mechanism: Once an ad works, the concept is validated; producing near-identical variants with a few changed elements is higher-expected-value than inventing fresh concepts.
tactics.evidence: Assertion from his own practice ('this works really well... once I land on an ad that I like').

rscFit.reasoning: Correct strategy, already held.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate — the instruction to produce many deliberate iterations of a dissected winner and to ask the model for ten more variants around a hook that landed is already recorded; this is the same claim reworded as an LLM prompt.

tactics.claim: Generate a detailed full-lineup product shot with some units in branded packaging and one or two unboxed, earthy brand props alongside, shallow depth of field, warm natural window light, on a nice-but-not-luxurious counter.
tactics.mechanism: One frame shows everything in the range plus how the packaging looks on arrival, and the shallow depth of field plus warm light makes it read as a real lifestyle photo rather than a catalogue render.
tactics.evidence: Assertion only; given as a long verbatim worked prompt.

rscFit.reasoning: Duplicate of recorded lever lists and generation guidance.

tactics.rejectReason: marketing-product-image-stack already holds the main-image lever list including the product shown alongside its packaging and everything included in a multipack, plus fixing a brand visual identity once; marketing-ai-product-imagery already covers generating the lifestyle-in-a-room shot. The only unrecorded detail — the realism ceiling — is adopted as its own tactic.
